## Conclusion

The claim is **well-supported by strong evidence**. In a multicenter, randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial published in the *New England Journal of Medicine* (Devinsky et al., 2017), 120 children and young adults with drug-resistant Dravet syndrome received add-on cannabidiol (CBD, up to 20 mg/kg/day) or placebo alongside their standard antiepileptic regimen. Over 14 weeks, the median monthly frequency of convulsive seizures fell from 12.4 to 5.9 with CBD, compared to a decline from 14.9 to 14.1 with placebo—a statistically significant reduction attributable to CBD (https://www.nejm.org/doi/full/10.1056/NEJMoa1611618).

This finding was corroborated by a subsequent dose-ranging trial (published in *Neurology*, 2018) confirming efficacy across two CBD doses versus placebo, and by a 2020 randomized trial in *JAMA Neurology* that similarly found both tested CBD doses significantly reduced convulsive seizure frequency compared with placebo (https://jamanetwork.com/journals/jamaneurology/fullarticle/2762458). A 2020 systematic review in *CNS Drugs* further synthesized these adjunctive CBD trials, concluding a consistent seizure-reduction benefit in Dravet syndrome, alongside a recognized side-effect profile including somatotherapy such as diarrhea, somnolence, and elevated liver enzymes, particularly when combined with valproate (https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40263-020-00708-6). Long-term open-label follow-up data also indicate the benefit is sustained over time.

This body of high-quality randomized controlled trial evidence led the FDA to approve purified CBD (Epidiolex) specifically as an adjunctive treatment for Dravet syndrome-associated seizures in 2018.

**Bottom line:** The claim is accurate—add-on CBD reduces convulsive seizure frequency in children with Dravet syndrome, based on robust RCT evidence, though it carries notable side effects requiring monitoring.
